tríkāladarśin [darśin] amnf trikāladarśinī omniscient — m. wise; prophet.
tríkāladṛṣṭi | dṛṣṭi | f. omniscience.

tríkūṭa [kūṭa] amnf Trikūṭā which has 3 summits; said of various mountains | not. three peaks of the Maṇika Mountains range in the district of Jammu, where the cave of Vaisno Devī is located | arch. said of a temple with three sanctuaries | myth. np. of Trikūta, mountain "with three peaks", surrounded by the ocean of milk [kṣīrodadhi]; Varuṇa resides there in the Rtumat grove | geo. np. of the city of Trikūṭa₁, north of Konkana, capital of the Traikūṭaka dynasty — f. trikūtā myth. np. of Trikūtā, little girl who at 9 years old begged Rāma to marry her; He gave her the name Vaisnavī and promised to marry her when he was reborn as Kalkī; she is worshipped in the cave temple of Vaisno Devī, in the district of Jammu, 12 km above Katra.
tríkona | kona | n. triangle; syn. tribhuja. vahnitrikonam n. phil. [Tantra] triangle with the point upwards, symbolizing the male principle in a dia
geometric gram [yantra]. śaktitrikonam n. phil. [Tantra] triangle with the point downwards, symbolizing the feminine principle in a dia
geometric gram [yantra].
trikharva [kharva] n. math. ten trillion; syn. śańkha, hāhā.

trigata [gata] n. soc. ["conversation for three"] burlesque farce played by the vidūṣaka, the sūtradhāra and his assistant [pāripārśvika] during the preliminaries of a play [pūrvaraṅga]; they employ the ganda (quick-witted repartee), nālikā (riddles) and asatpralāpa (verbal delirium) methods.

trigarta [garta] m. geo. country of the Trigarta | pl. [Mah.] np. of the Trigartās people; their kingdom was northwest of that of the Kauravās, between the Vipāśā and the Satadru; their king was Suśarmā; allies of the Kau ravās, they attacked the kingdom of Virāṭa to steal his cattle; their princes were defeated by their sworn enemy Arjuna | man or prince of this people. triguņa | guṇa | n. the triple — m. pl. phil. [Sāṃkhya] the triad of the three essences or qualities of nature: the Pure Essence of Being [sattva] (purity, truth), Passion [rajas] (strength, desire) and Darkness [tamas] (ignorance, inertia) — amnf triguṇā triple | (twist, cable) made of three strands — adv. triguṇā triply. trigunam in three ways. trigunākaroti he plows for the 3rd time. triguņasāmya [sāmya] n. phil. [Sāṃkhya] balance of the three qualities of primordial Nature [pradhāna]; cf. Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya.

triguṇātīta [atīta] amnf triguṇātītā phil. appeared beyond the three qualities of Nature. triguṇātītya phil. having disappeared beyond the three essences. trighanța [ghanțā] m. lit. [KSS.] np. of the peak of the Himalayas Trighanta, capital of the rākṣasa king Lam bajihva.
tricatvāriṃśa [catvāriṃśa] amnf tricatvāriṃśī ord. 43ᵉ.
tricatvārimsat [catvārimsat] f. 43.
trícīvara [cīvara] n. bd. the triple habit of the monk: antaravāsaka, uttarāsanga and samghāṭi.
tríjagat [jagat] n. cf. triloka.
tríjaṭa [jaṭa] amnf trijaṭā who wears 3 chignons — f. trijaṭā myth. [Rām.] np. of the rākṣasī trijaṭā, guard and friend of Sītā during her captivity.
tríjīvā [jīvā] f. cf. trijyā.
tríjyā [jyā₃] f. math. radius of a circle (as sine of a 90° angle = 3×30).
trijyākā [ka] f. cf. trijyā.
tritva [tva] n. triad, Trinity.
tridanda |danda| n. phil. the triple control of one's thoughts, words and actions | soc. the three staffs of an ascetic [parivrājaka]; they are bound at one end, and can be opened to form a tripod.
tridandaka [ka| n. id.

tridandin [in] m. soc. ascetic [parivrājaka] por tant the three sticks; not. renunciant of the order of Rāmānuja | myth. np. of Tridaṇḍī "Father whip d", a bālagraha; he sticks out his tongue |lalajjihva|.
trídaśa [daśan] amnf tridaśī pl. 30 | myth. the 30 gods.
tridasyu |dasyu| mr. myth. n.p. of the sage Trida syu, son of Agasti and Lopāmudrā; cf. Idhmavāha, Drdhadasyu.
tridosa | dosa₂ | m. med. one of the three humors of the body: bile [pitta], breath [vāyu] and phlegm [kapha]; cf. triphalā, tridhātu.
tridhanvan [dhanvan] m. myth. n.p. of Tridhanvā "of the three bows", king of Ayodhyā of the solar lineage, son of Vasumanā; he is father of Trayyāruņa.
tridhātu |dhātu| amnf tripartite — m. soc. oblation in 3 parts — n. 3 metals | med. the 3 humors; cf. tridoșa.
trínavata | navata | amnf trinavatī ord. 93°.
trínavati |navati| f. 93.
trinavatitama [tama] amnf trinavatitamī ord. 93ᵉ.
trínātha [nātha] m. phil. the Hindu Trinity: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, SivaMaheśvara; syn. trimūrti.
trināthamandira | mandira | m. small neighborhood or village temple, serving as a shelter and meeting place, often near a sacred tree, including a shrine dedicated to the Trinity | trinātha|.
trínetra | netra | amnf trinetrā f. trinetrī who has three eyes (epith. of Shiva); syn. tryambaka.
trípañcāśá [pañcāśa] amnf tripañcāśī ord. 53°.
trípañcāśat [pañcāśat] f. 53.
trípatāka [patāka] amnf tripatākā refers to the ritual gesture |mudrā| of the triple banner (hand with three fingers extended).
tripatha [patha] m. with 3 paths.
tripathagā [gā₁] f. myth. "which flows in three courses", epith. of the Gangā; syn. trisrotas; cf. triveni.
tripád |pad₂| amnf |noun. tripād| tripod;
tripod | which takes 3 steps | tripartite.
trípada | pada | amnf tripadā with 3 feet; with 3 words | lit. (stanza) with 3 divisions.
tripari | bet | ind. missed three (not. in the game pañcaka).
tripāṭhin | pāṭhin | amnf tripāṭhinī who masters 3 Vedas.

trípāda [pāda] m. tripod; triple asterism — f. tripādī gram. set of the last three sections of the Aṣṭādhyāyī (from the second section of the eighth book); their rules are applied sequentially as a last resort; syn. asiddhakāṇḍa; opp. sapādasaptādhyāyī.

trípiṭaka [piṭaka] mn bd. the "three baskets", works constituting the canon of the doctrine: the canonical teaching [sūtrāṇi], the monastic rule [vinaya] and the philosophical doctrine [abhidharma] pali tipitaka.
trípindī [pinda] f. soc. offering of the 3 dumplings (to the three closest ancestors); at the death of the father, a fourth is divided into three.
tríputa [puṭa] amnf tripuṭā triple; triangular — m. mus. rhythmic cycle [tāla] comprising 1 laghu and 2 druta.
triputaka [ka] m. triangle.
tripundra [pundra] n. soc. Shaivite sectarian mark consisting of 3 horizontal lines of ash or sandalwood on the forehead.
tripundraka |ka| n. id.

triputra | putra | m. father of three sons. na hi triputro dviputra iti kathyate (maxim) One cannot say of a father of three sons that he is the father of two sons; Patanjali₁ uses it to explain Pan (6,4,96).

Tripura | Pura | n. myth. np. of the Tripura fortress "triple city", a set of three cities built in the clouds by Maya for the demons |asura|, of gold in Heaven, silver in the atmosphere, and iron on Earth; the three cities moved, and were only exceptionally aligned; it was destroyed by Shiva Pinakin; it symbolizes the illusion of the phenomenal world, destroyed by the divine knowledge of the yogi; [Mah.] When the dai tya Taraka was killed by Kartikeya, his three sons Taraksa, Vidyunmali, and Kamalaksa performed great penances and obtained from Brahma the right to take refuge in three celestial cities made of iron [Ayasmayi], silver, and gold, and to perish only after a thousand years, by a single arrow; they then committed great sacrileges, and the gods implored Shiva to put an end to their crimes; Shiva acquired half the power of all the gods and became Mahada; he used the magic bow Saivacapa made for him by Vishvakarma and made Vishnu the arrow that destroyed Tripura and his demons; Brahma drove his chariot; the three cities symbolize the three bodies [śarīra] sources of our ignorance; cf. Pura, Tripuraghna, Tripurāri.
Tripuraghna | ghna | mr. myth. n.p. of Tripuraghna, epith. of Siva "Destroyer of Tripura".
tripuradāha [dāha] m. myth. destruction by fire of Tripura.
tripurasundarī [sundarī] f. myth. np. of Tripu rasundarī or Tripurā "Splendor beyond mi rage", form of the Goddess worshipped with the śrīcakra (śrīvidyā); cf. Lalitā.
tripurāntaka [antaka] m. myth. np. of Tri purāntaka, epith. of Siva "Destroyer of Tripu ra".
Tripurāri [ari] m. myth. np. of Tripurāri, epith. of Siva "Enemy of Tripura".
tripurusa [tripurusa] n. period of 3 generations. tripurusam adv. for 3 generations.
triphalā [phalā] f. the three myrobalans, mixture of the fruits of the āmalakī, the vibhītakī and the harītakī, used in traditional medicine [Ayurveda] to treat the three humors | tridoṣa|.
tribhanga | bhanga | amnf tribhangī describes the posture "in triple bend", the body resting asymmetrically on one leg.
Tribhāṣyaratna [bhāṣyaratna] n. bed. n.p. Tribhāsyaratna, commentary on the Tait of the tirīyaprātiśākhya due to Somayārya.
tribhuj [bhuj₃] amnf in three parts.

tríbhuja [bhuja] amnf tribhujā triangular — m. math. triangle; syn. trikona. samatribhuja m. math. equilateral triangle. svarnatribhuja geo. golden triangle of Orissa, defined by Bhuvaneśvarī₁, Purī and Koṇārka.
tríbhuvana [bhuvana] n. cf. triloka.

tribhuvanamaheśvara [Maheśvara] m. myth. n.p. from the tribhuvanamaheśvara temple in Iśvarapura (mod. Banteay Srei in Cambodia); it was built by the advisor Yajñavarāha of king Yajñavarmā₅ and consecrated in 967.
tribhuvaneśvara [īśvara] m. myth. np. of Trib huvaneśvara, epith. of Shiva "Lord of the three Worlds"; he is worshipped in Bhuvaneśvarī₁ as Lingarāja.
tribhuvādityavarman [ādityavarman] m. hist. n.p. of the Khmer king Tribhuvādityavarmā (12th century).
tríbhūma [bhūma] amnf tribhūmā three-tiered.
tríbhauma | bhauma | amnf three-story tribhaumā.

trímala [mala] amnf trimalā phil. [śaiva] affected by the three defilements — mn pl. phil. the three original sins, arising from ignorance [avidyā]; the gross sin |sthūla| is kārmamala, of believing in one's free will; it is due to the action which provokes impressions, such as pleasure and pain; the subtle sin [sūkṣma] is māyīyamala, of considering one's body and possessions as one's self; the very subtle sin [para] is āṇavamala, which reduces consciousness to a finite limit.
trímārga [mārga] m. phil. [yoga] the triple path of spiritual realization: karmayoga, bhaktiyoga and jñānayoga.
trímuni [muni] ind. gram. (n.) triad of Sages of the Sanskrit grammatical tradition (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana and Patanjali₁); syn. munitraya.
trímūrti [mūrti] amnf which has three forms — m. phil. the Hindu Trinity: Brahmā, Visnu, Siva Maheśvara; the trio of resp. Candra, Dattātreya and Durvāsā is its incarnation; syn. trinātha.

tríratna [ratna] n. bd. the "3 jewels" of the trinity: Buddha, his Law [dharma] and his Community [sangha] | arch. bd. emblematic trifoliate motif of the 3 jewels | phil. [Tantra] the triplet of thought, breath and semen; their cessation brings liberation.
trírāśi | rāśi | iic. 3 signs of the zodiac.
trírāśipa [pa₂] amnf trirāśipā astr. Who rules 3 signs of the zodiac.
trírūpa [rūpa] amnf trirūpā Which has three forms or colors.

trilakṣaṇa [lakṣaṇa] n. bd. [Yogācāra] doctrine of the three characteristics of logical reason [hetu]; the first is impermanence [anityatā] || pali tilakkhana. trîlinga [linga] amnf trilingī That which possesses the 3 qualities | gram. adjective (That which admits the 3 genders) | one of the three signs [linga]: Bhīmeśvara at Dakṣārāma, Mallikārjuna Mahālinga at Srīśaila, and Kāleśvara₁ — n. [trilingadeśa] geo. np. of the Telinga or Telingana country delimited by these three pilgrimage sites — m. pl. geo. people of the Telinga country; cf. Tailanga — f. trilingī gram. the three genders.
trilingajanapada [janapada] m. cf. trilingadeśa.
trilingadesa [desa] mn geo. Telinga country, Telugu language; cf. Andhra.
tríloka [loka] mn pl. myth. the three worlds: heaven [svarga], earth [bhūmi], and hell [pātāla]; syn. tribhuvana — f. cf. trilokī.
trílocana [locana] m. myth. np. of Trilocana, epith. of Shiva "with three eyes".

trilocanasiva [Siva] m. hist. n.p. of the theologian śaiva trilocanaśiva ācārya ; he lived in South India in the 12th century; we owe him the Prāyaścittasamuccaya, the Siddhāntasārāvalī, the Dhyānaratnāvalī and the Somaśambhupaddhatiţīkā.
trivamsa [vamsa] m. together of the three upper castes: brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya.
trivandhura [vandhura] amnf trivandhurā That which can seat 3 people; notably qualifies the chariot of the Aśvinau.

trivarga [varga] m. phil. division of human activities into three domains, corresponding to the three goals of man on earth: duty [dharma], wealth [artha], and pleasure [kāma]; cf. puruṣārtha | lit. induced division of the ensei
gnements [śāstra] in dharmaśāstra, arthaśāstra and kāmaśāstra.
trivarna [varna] amnf trivarnā with three colors — m. soc. set of the three upper classes: brāhmaņa, kṣatriya and vaiśya.
trivali |vali| amnf Which forms 3 folds — f. var. trivalī the 3 folds above a woman's navel, a sign of classical beauty in poetry.

Trivikrama | vikrama | m. ved. np. of Trivikrama "He who takes three strides", epith. of Vishnu as an aspect of the Sun traversing the sky | myth. (later) epith. of Vishnu under the aspect of his avatar Vāmana, Who traversed the universe (the three worlds) in three steps to dispossess the demon king Bali; at the 1st step, he covered the whole earth, at the 2nd, he took the sky and the universe, and at the 3rd, placing his heel on Bali's forehead, he drove him into the irons; he is represented with his left leg vertical; he is the model of the victorious king, Who conquers his empire with ease; cf. Urukrama hist. np. of Trivikrama₁ Bhatta, court poet of the emperor Rāstrakūta Indra₃ (10th century); He is the author of Nalacampū, a precursor of the genre
campū [adicampūkāvya] | hist. n.p. by Trivikrama₂ (11th century), author of the Tātparyaṭīka₁ commentary on the Vṛttaratnākara | hist. n.p. from the prākṛta grammarian Trivikrama₃ (13th century).
trivikramasena [senā] m. lit. [VeP.] np. of King Tri vikramasena of Pratisthāna; he listens to the stories of the undead |vetāla| and solves his riddles.
trividya | vidyā| amnf trividyā lit. That which contains the 3 Vedas.
trivistapa [viṣṭapa] n. myth. sky of Indra; syn. svarga.
trivṛt |vṛt₂| amnf triple.
tríveni |veni | f. geo. triple confluence of the Gangā and Yamunā rivers with the underground Sarasvatī₁; cf. Prayāga | var. triveṇī id.
triveda | veda | mr. bed. the triple veda: Rgveda, Ya jurveda, Sāmaveda.
trívedin [vedin] amnf trivedinī soc. (brah mane) Who knows the triple veda.

tríśanku | śanku | m. myth. np. of the king of Ayodhyā Triśańku; born Satyavrata₂, he is the son of King Trayyāruņa of the solar lineage [sūryavaṃśa]; he led a dissolute youth; as he had disrupted the marriage of a brahmin and abducted the bride, his father repudiated him at the request of the chaplain Vasistha, and he went to live with the untouchables [caṇḍāla] in the forest; Trayyāruṇa left his palace to do penance in the forest, in order to have another heir; as punishment for having exiled his son, his country was afflicted with 12 years of drought; Viśvāmitra's family suffered from this, and his wife took their son Gālava to the market to sell him for food; Satyavrata was moved by this, and provided for the family with the products of his hunting; one evening, having found no game all day, he reached the hermitage of Vasistha, whom he hated; he killed his abundant cow Nandinī, ate some of it, and offered the rest to Viśvāmitra's family; when Vasistha learned of this, he cursed him for his three sins (offending his father, abducting a brahmin's wife, and eating cow), degraded him to a caṇḍāla, and gave him the name Triśańku "In the throes of three sins"; cursed by all, he prepared a pyre to throw himself on; As he prayed to the Goddess before dying, she told him that he would become king; Nārada informed the king, who abdicated in favor of Triśanku and went into exile in the forest; Triśanku reigned wisely, and performed penances in order to ascend to heaven with his mortal body; |Rām.| he begged Vasistha to perform the rites, but the latter refused, for no text provided for this consecration [yāga]; then he prayed to the 100 sons of Vasistha, who mocked him; faced with his arrogance they cursed him and degraded him again to candāla; deposed from his status, he abdicated the throne of Ayodhyā and his son Hariścandra succeeded him; Triśanku returned to the forest, where Viśvāmitra met him, returning from penance; In gratitude for his help to his family, he led a great sacrifice |yāga|, despite Vasistha's opposition; Triśańku ascended to heaven [svarga], but the gods refused this caṇḍāla, and hurled him down to Earth; he was stopped in his fall by Viśvāmitra, who fixed him in the sky as the Southern Cross, in a constellation he created for him; there he reigns with his mortal candāla body, upside down, in a kingdom that is neither earthly nor heavenly | (by analogy) paradoxical condition, if ambiguous | myth. [Rām.] King Triśańku is said to be the son of Pṛthu₁ and the father of Dhundhumāra | bd. np. of the caṇḍāla chief Triśaṅku₁; cf. Śārdūlakarṇa. Triśańkurivāntarā tiṣṭhaḥ tienstoi entre les deux, comme Triśanku. Triśańkusvarga | svarga | m. myth. the sky of Triśańku, which is neither celestial nor terrestrial | by extension an ambiguous notion.

triśata | śata | n. 103 — amnf Triśatī ord. 300° — m. pl. 300 — f. Triśati 300 | bed. n.p. of the Trisatī or Trisatikā, epith. from the treatise Pātīgaņita of Śrīdharācārya “in 300 verses”. trišikha | śikhā | amnf trišikhā with three vertices — n. trident.

triśiras | śiras | amnf three-headed; syn. triśīrṣan — m. ved. np. of Triśirā "three-headed", monster made by his father the celestial craftsman Tvastā; one of his heads drank the soma and read the Veda, another drank the surā, the third was eager to drink the Universe; [Mah.] his three faces burned like the Sun, the Moon, and Fire; he practiced severe asceticism, and his power was immense; Indra, threatened in his supremacy, tried in vain to have him seduced by the nymphs |apsarasas|; he struck him down with his vajra, but his energy confessed to him, and burned even after his death; he then gave a carpenter to cut off his heads with his axe; He did so only after Indra had identified himself and promised to be the future recipient of the heads of sacrificed beasts; from the three heads came pheasants, partridges, and sparrows; to atone for his brahmanicide [brahmahatyā], Šiva forced Indra to practice harsh asceticism with the divine breaths [marut], and to distribute his guilt among the Earth, the Ocean, the trees, and the women, to whom he granted corresponding gifts; to avenge Triśirā, his father Tvaṣṭā created the asura Vṛṭra; cf. Tvāṣṭra, Viśvarūpa.

triśīrsan [śīrṣan] amn three-headed — m. myth. np. of Triśīrṣā "three-headed", epith. of Tvāṣṭra |var. Triśīrṣa lit. [KSS.] np. of the cave of Triśīrṣa which connects the North and South faces of Kailāsa, and which Naravāhanadatta must cross; it is guarded by Kālarātri.

triśūla [śūla] n. trident | myth. Shiva's trident, fashioned by Viśvakarmā from the shavings obtained by planing the Sun's brilliance; its three points | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | sance [jñāna] and activity [kriyā], the three attributes of Bhairava.

trísasti |sasti| f. 63; syn. trayahsasti. trișașțiśalākāpurușacaritra | śalākāpurușacaritra | n. lit. np. from Trișașțiśalākāpurușacaritra "Biographies of the 63 illustrious people (of Jainism)" by Hemacandra.
trísapta |sapta| num. pers. pl. three times seven | trisapta ved. id.
trísaptata |saptata| amnf trisaptatī ord. 73ᵉ.
trísaptati |saptati| f. 73.
trisaptatitama [tama] amnf trisaptatitamī ord. 73ᵉ.
trístana | stana | amnf tristanī which has three nipples — f. tristanī woman with 3 breasts | cow with 3 teats.
trísthāna |sthāna| amnf tristhānā which has three locations | which resides In the three worlds — n. phil. |yoga| the three points of attention: posture [āsana], breathing [prāṇa] and focus [dṛṣṭi].
trísrotas [srotas] f. myth. "which flows in three courses", epith. of Gangā; syn. tripathagā; cf. triveni.

trisvabhāva | svabhāva | m. bd. | Yogācāra | doctrine of the threefold nature of reality: illusory reality is imaginary | parikalpita|; relative reality is dependent | paratantra|, and source of errors; absolute reality is ultimate | parinispanna| and not cryptible; syn. trilakṣaṇa.

trisvabhāvanirdeśa | nirdeśa | mr. bed. n.p. from Vasubandhu's Tris vabhāvanirdeśa; There he developed the idealist doctrine [vijñānavāda] of the Yogācāra Buddhist school. trîhāyaṇa |hāyana| amnf trihāyaṇī aged 3 years.
trimśa [tridaśa] amnf trimśī ord. 30th |+30 — m. bed. stoma in 30 parts.
trimśaka |ka| amnf trimśikā in 30 parts; of value 30 — f. trimśikā lit. np. of the trimśikā "30 verses", treatise on logic by Vasubandhu | cf. parātrimśikā.
triṃśát [triṃśa] num. f. sg. thirty | var. trimsati id. trimśattama var. trimśa, trimśatī |tama| amnf trimśattamī ord. thirtieth.

trimśatsāhasra [sāhasra] amnf trimśatsāhasrā f. trimśatsāhasrī pl. 30000. kalau trimsatsāhasrāņi Visņus tisthati bhūtale In the era of Kali, Vișnu remains on Earth for 30000 years. রিক triká [trika] amnf trikā triple, tripartite | occurring for the 3rd time — n. triad; sorting

nity | lumbar region | phon. system of description of meters by triads due to Pingala₂ | phil. np. of Trika "Trinity", tantric doctrine of the unity between the three divine energies: the desire [icchā] of the
subject [pramātr], knowledge [jñāna] of knowledge [pramāṇa], and the activity [kriyā] of the object to be known [prameya]; this Trinity is symbolized by the tri
tooth [triśūla] of Bhairava; cf. trikaśāstra — m. in intersection of 3 roads.

trikaśāstra [śāstra] n. phil. triple system [Trika] of non-dual [advaita] Shaivism of Kaśmīra as taught by Abhinavagupta; it posits three levels of reality: the supreme transcendent Shiva, the immanent creative energy Shakti, and the individual microcosm [anu] of man [nara] to be liberated; this triad is also taught as identification with the supreme |para|, identity in difference [parāpara], and the differentiated lower human condition [apara₂]; also as the three states of creation [sṛṣṭi], preservation [sthiti], and
destruction |saṃhāra|, and the three divine energies Parā, Parāparā and Aparā; cf. anuttara, Tantrāloka.
trikasūtra |sūtra| n. bed. n.p. from the trikasūtra "Aphorism of the Trika", epith. of the Parātrīśikā tantra.

tritá [trita] m. myth. ved. np. of Trita "Third", spirit of the waters [āptya₂], ally of Indra whom he helped to defeat Viśvarūpa, in order to take upon himself the sin of brahmanicide | brahmahan | ; he is charged with preparing the soma; |Mah.| he is said to be ṛṣi, and son of Gautama; wandering thirsty with his brothers Ekata and Dvita, he found a well, but when he drew up the water from it his brothers pushed him in; he found the means to prepare the soma at the bottom of the well to offer it to the gods in order to be freed | gr. o .
